summary: Introduces and discusses issues in the design of accounting systems, which collect resource consumption data for capacity planning, cost allocation, auditing, and billing. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Accounting management records who used which network resources and when. RFC 2975 explains why a planning report can tolerate some missing data while billing and auditing may need stronger safeguards.

questions: how do you make accounting reliable
subtitle: Design choices for collecting, protecting and retaining network usage records.

tldr.problem: Accounting systems collect resource-use data for planning, cost allocation, auditing and billing. These applications need different levels of reliability, security and speed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo compares accounting objectives, failure protections, data-collection models and protocols such as RADIUS, TACACS+ and SNMP. It emphasizes matching system design to the application's needs.
tldr.outcome: No single protocol or security setup meets every accounting need. RFC 2975 is an Informational guide to the available design choices.

facts.label: Accounting objectives
facts.value: Capacity and trend analysis, cost allocation, auditing and billing

facts.label: Collection models
facts.value: Polling, event-driven, event-driven batching and event-driven polling

today: RFC 2975 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Accounting Data Is For
sections.content:
Accounting management collects resource-consumption data for capacity and trend analysis, cost allocation, auditing and billing. The data may be measured, rated, assigned and shared with the appropriate parties.

The memo distinguishes archival accounting, which aims to collect and retain data and reconstruct missing records, from applications that can accept some data loss. Since use cases differ in reliability and security needs, the goal is a set of tools rather than one universal protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Network accounting is a record of resource use. The system needs depend on whether the records are for rough planning or for financial and legal decisions.

sections.title: Different Goals Need Different Guarantees
sections.content:
Capacity planning and trend analysis can often tolerate moderate packet loss because they estimate future use. Usage-sensitive billing, auditing and cost allocation may need archival records, stronger reliability and security, and limits on processing delay.

Intra-domain records remain within one administrative organization, where packet loss may be lower and parties may trust one another. Inter-domain records cross organizational boundaries, where packet loss may be higher and the parties cannot be assumed to trust each other.
sections.plainLanguage: A missed record may barely affect a planning estimate, but it can change a bill. Records sent to another organization also need protection across that boundary.

sections.title: Reliability and Failure Recovery
sections.content:
The memo considers packet loss, accounting-server failure, network failure and device reboot. It stresses that transport retransmission alone cannot protect against server outages or network partitions. Non-volatile storage can preserve records through those failures.

Other tools include interim records, duplicate elimination, secondary servers and application-layer acknowledgments. An application acknowledgment means the accounting application has accepted responsibility for the data, not merely that the transport delivered it. A proxy that acknowledges before the server does can reduce reliability.
sections.plainLanguage: Retries cannot recover a record that disappears when a device reboots. Save important records in persistent storage and confirm that the accounting application accepted them.

sections.title: Four Ways to Collect Records
sections.content:
In polling, a manager asks devices for records at intervals; this supports batching but can add delay. An event-driven device sends records when events occur; sending each event separately reduces delay but is less efficient and may scale poorly.

Event-driven batching sends groups of records, balancing transfer efficiency with delay. Event-driven polling sends a notification first and then lets the manager retrieve records. The memo describes different trade-offs in state, reliability, bandwidth and suitability for roaming.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can ask devices for records, or devices can report when records are ready. Sending records in batches saves overhead but can delay delivery.

sections.title: Protocols and Transfer Choices
sections.content:
The memo reviews RADIUS, TACACS+ and SNMP. RADIUS uses an event-driven model over UDP and can provide low processing delay, but reliability behavior varies and its response does not confirm that the accounting application stored the data. TACACS+ uses TCP and supports start, stop and interim update messages.

SNMP is widely used for intra-domain accounting, often with polling; notifications can support event-driven approaches. SMTP and file-transfer protocols can move session records between accounting servers. The memo says designers should select a combination based on each application's reliability, security, efficiency and timing requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS, TACACS+ and SNMP make different trade-offs. A system can also collect data one way and transfer completed records another way.
